turns.prompt_text: are there any open source pcbs with many tile tags or Apple Air tag like Hardware circuits
turns.response_html:
Yes, there are several open-source hardware projects and PCB designs that mimic the functionality of Apple AirTags or Tile tags, largely by utilizing the Nordic nRF52 series microcontrollers.

Key Open-Source Projects

  • OpenHaystack: This is the most popular framework for creating "DIY AirTags." It allows you to use the Apple Find My network on non-Apple hardware.
  • FakeTag: A lightweight project specifically designed for the nRF51822 to send location reports through the Find My system.
  • DIY AirTag (Circuit Digest): A complete hardware guide and PCB design based on the MDBT50Q-1MV2 (nRF52840) module. It includes a buzzer and accelerometer for motion detection.

Recommended Hardware/PCBs

If you want to build or order a PCB, these components and designs are standard:

Component TypePopular Open-Source ChoiceFeatures
MicrocontrollerNordic nRF52832 or nRF52840Low power, BLE 5.0+, and Find My support.
PCB DesignnRF52832-MDKA fully open-source micro development kit.
BatteryCR2032 Coin CellStandard for trackers due to size and 3V output.
SensorsADXL345Low-power accelerometer often used in Tile-like tags.

Where to find PCB files

  1. GitHub: Search for airtag-hardware or nRF52-tracker-pcb. Users like stacksmashing and adamcatley have documented AirTag reverse-engineering and hardware clones.
  2. OSHWLab: Search for "BLE Tracker" or "Find My" to find community-submitted KiCad or EasyEDA layouts ready for manufacturing.

turns.response_html:
Manufacturing 100 units of an open-source tracking tag (like an AirTag alternative) typically costs between $6.00 and $12.00 per unit for the hardware and assembly. This brings your total project estimate to roughly $600 – $1,200.

The final price depends heavily on whether you assemble them yourself or use a turnkey PCB assembly service.

Key Hardware for Your Order

To build these, you'll need bulk packs of the specialized surface-mount components:

  • Microcontroller: The nRF52832-QFAA-R is the industry standard for these trackers. In quantities of 100, the nRF52832 Module can be found for roughly $6.53 per module if pre-soldered, or closer to $1.85 for the bare chip.
  • Battery Holders: These CR2032 3V Battery Sockets are specifically designed for PCB mounting and are highly affordable in 100-packs.
  • Audio Alerts: To match AirTag functionality, Small Passive Piezo Buzzers are necessary for the "Find My" ping sounds.

Important Cost Considerations

  • Setup Fees: PCB assembly services often charge a one-time "Setup Fee" or "Stencil Fee" (usually $50–$150). This is why the price per unit drops significantly when you move from 10 units to 100.
  • Enclosures: These prices do not include a plastic case. You would likely need to 3D print these or order a custom injection-molded shell, which can add $1.00–$3.00 per unit at this scale.
  • Batteries: CR2032 batteries are usually purchased separately to avoid shipping restrictions (roughly $0.30–$0.50 each in bulk).

turns.prompt_text: Aldi's open source tile finders how long do they last or do they need another battery
turns.response_html:
Aldi typically sells these trackers under their Maginon or Bauhn house brands. While they aren't "open source" in the traditional software sense, they are built on standard hardware that often allows them to work across different tracking networks.

Here is the breakdown of how long they last and how to handle the batteries:

Battery Life & Replacement

Most Aldi smart tags use a standard CR2032 coin cell battery, which is the same one used in the Apple AirTag.

  • Standard Tags (Puck style): These generally last about 1 year with normal use. You do not need to buy a new tag; you simply pop the back cover off and swap in a fresh CR2032 battery.
  • Card Trackers (Wallet style): Some Aldi "Special Buys" include ultra-slim Bauhn Smart Tag Cards. These are unique because they are often rechargeable via USB-C, lasting several months per charge, rather than using disposable batteries.
  • Low Battery Alerts: If you use the Maginon tags with the Apple "Find My" app, your iPhone will send you a notification when the battery is getting low.

Are they actually Open Source?

Technically, no. They are commercial products with proprietary firmware. However, they are popular in the "open hardware" community because:

  1. Network Flexibility: Many Aldi tags (like the Maginon Smart Tag Duo) are designed to work with both Apple Find My and Google Find My Device, which is rare.
  2. Familiar Hardware: They often use the same Nordic nRF52 chips found in open-source projects like OpenHaystack, making them a favorite for hobbyists who want to "flash" their own custom firmware onto cheap, pre-built hardware.

turns.prompt_text: is there a way to use these tags to find them using a network so that when the tools are when the air tags are near each other they can know where their location is but not individually
turns.response_html:
Yes, it is possible to set up a system where tags track each other’s proximity without exposing their individual identities to a central server. This is often referred to as Collaborative Tracking or a Decentralized Mesh Network.

While Apple’s official "Find My" network is designed to report individual tag locations to a single owner, you can use the open-source hardware mentioned earlier to build a more private, group-based system.

How to Achieve "Collective" Tracking

To have tags know they are "near each other" without tracking them individually, you would shift from a Broadcast model to a Mesh model.

  • BLE Mesh Networking: Instead of each tag talking to a phone, the tags talk to each other. You can program nRF52-based PCBs to form a Bluetooth Mesh.
  • Proximity Logic: You can write a script where a tag only "alerts" or logs a location if it detects a specific number of "sibling" tags nearby. If a tag is alone, it stays silent.
  • Privacy-Preserving Keys: Using a framework like OpenHaystack, you can generate a shared group key. Instead of 100 different IDs, all 100 tags could broadcast the same "group ID." You would know a tool from the kit is nearby, but not necessarily which one.

Popular Open-Source Frameworks for This

ProjectHow it works for your goal
OpenHaystackCan be modified to have multiple tags share a single "Public Key" so they appear as one collective entity on a map.
Wirepas MassiveAn enterprise-grade decentralized mesh that allows tags to "talk" to each other to determine density and location without a central hub.
ESP32-BLE-CollectorA project that can be used to create a "hub" that only reports if it sees a specific combination of tags together.

Practical Example: The "Toolbox" Scenario

If you have a fleet of tools and only want to know if the entire kit is at a job site:

  1. Program each tag to broadcast a "Group ID."
  2. Use a single "Master Tag" or a smartphone app set to Proximity Mode.
  3. The system only marks the location as "Complete" if it hears pings from 10+ tags at once.

This prevents you from being "tracked" by your individual items while still ensuring the collective group is where it should be.

turns.prompt_text: please compare and contrast the difference between using a mesh
turns.response_html:
In the context of hardware tracking tags, switching from a Star Network (like AirTags or Tile) to a Mesh Network (like Bluetooth Mesh or Thread) changes how devices talk to each other and how they report their presence.

The core difference is that in a Star Network, every tag is an "island" that must talk to a central hub (your phone) to be found. In a Mesh Network, the tags "cooperate" by passing messages to one another.

Comparison: Star vs. Mesh for Tracking

FeatureStar Network (AirTag/Tile)Mesh Network (nRF52 Mesh)
CommunicationTag $\rightarrow$ Hub (Phone/Router)Tag $\leftrightarrow$ Tag $\leftrightarrow$ Hub
ReliabilityFails if the tag is too far from a phone.If one tag can't reach a phone, it can "hop" its signal through other tags.
Battery LifeHigh. Tags sleep most of the time.Low. Nodes often stay "awake" to relay signals for others.
ScaleBest for individual personal items.Best for industrial assets (toolboxes, warehouses).
ComplexitySimple: Plug and play.High: Requires custom firmware and network "provisioning."

Why use a Mesh Network?

The primary reason to use mesh for your tool tracking project is coverage expansion without extra hubs.

  • Self-Healing: If you have 50 tools in a large workshop, and only one tool is near the exit door (where a receiver is), that tool can act as a bridge for all the tools at the back of the shop. If you move that "bridge" tool, the network automatically finds a new path.
  • Collective Awareness: In a mesh, the tags can be programmed to perform "Presence Logic." For example, a "Master Tag" on a toolbox can scan for its "Sub-Tags" (the tools). If the toolbox moves but doesn't hear from all its sub-tags, the toolbox itself can trigger an alarm.
  • Reduced Infrastructure: You don't need a phone or a WiFi router in every corner of a building; you just need enough tags to stay within range of each other.

Why stick with a Star (Traditional) Network?

  • Extreme Battery Savings: Because an AirTag-style device only broadcasts and never has to "listen" for other tags, it can last over a year on a tiny battery. A "relay" node in a mesh network typically drains a battery in weeks or months unless it is carefully optimized or plugged into power.
  • Privacy: In a traditional network, tags don't know each other exist. In a mesh, every node technically knows about the traffic of its neighbors, which requires much more complex encryption to keep private.

Summary Recommendation

  • Use a Star Network if you want to track individual items that might be anywhere in the world (using the massive network of other people's iPhones).
  • Use a Mesh Network if you want to track a collection of items within a specific local area (like a construction site or a film set) where the items need to "watch out" for each other.
